paras: The Greensboro police whipping was the whipping of a number of Black people by a policeman in Greensboro, North Carolina, in early August 1890, as punishment for fighting. It is known from a single line in the Asheville Daily Citizen, which described the policeman as "properly delegated" and gave no names, number of victims or exact date.

According to the Asheville Daily Citizen of 8 August 1890, "negroes" at Greensboro had been whipped "a day or ago" (probably "a day or two ago") by a policeman. The stated reason was that they had been fighting; the item does not say with whom, where in the town, or how many were whipped. Nor does it say who had delegated the policeman or under what sentence or order he acted.
No report of any complaint, inquiry or other official response to the whipping appears in the coverage.

The whipping reached print as one unheadlined sentence in the Citizen's column "The Latest News from North Carolina," set between a store fire at Burlington and a notice of revival meetings at Winston. Its wording, a policeman "properly delegated," presented the punishment as authorized and routine rather than as an abuse. No other white paper and no Black paper was found to report the episode, so the only version is the brief white-press notice.
